metadata.examTitle: Designing and Implementing Microsoft DevOps Solutions
metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Companion for AZ-400 certification - validates expertise in designing and implementing DevOps practices for version control, compliance, infrastructure as code, configuration management, and continuous integration/delivery.

questions.title: Branching Strategy Selection
questions.scenario: A development team of 20 developers works on a web application with bi-weekly releases. They need a branching strategy that supports feature isolation, code reviews, and stable releases.
questions.questionText: Which branching strategy should you recommend?

choices.text: GitHub Flow with feature branches and pull requests
Single main branch with direct commits
Trunk-based development with no branches
GitFlow with develop, release, and hotfix branches

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which approach balances feature isolation and code review without adding unnecessary branch complexity?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GitHub Flow uses short-lived feature branches merged to main via pull requests. It's simpler than GitFlow while providing isolation for features and mandatory code reviews. With bi-weekly releases, the lightweight approach is preferable to GitFlow's complexity.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GitHub Flow: main + feature branches; deploy from main.
  • GitFlow: main, develop, feature, release, hotfix branches; more complex.
  • Trunk-based: very short branches or direct commits; requires mature CI/CD.
  • Choose based on release frequency and team maturity.

questions.title: Pull Request Policies
questions.scenario: Your team needs to enforce code quality standards before merging. Requirements: at least two reviewers must approve, builds must pass, and work items must be linked.
questions.questionText: How should you configure the repository?

choices.text: Branch policies with required reviewers, build validation, and work item linking
Rely on developers to follow guidelines manually
Post-merge code reviews
Disable direct pushes without any other controls

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about what can enforce requirements automatically rather than relying on human discipline.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure DevOps branch policies enforce requirements before PR completion. Configure minimum reviewer count (2), require passing build validation, and require linked work items. This automates quality gates and ensures compliance without manual enforcement.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Branch policies can require specific reviewers for certain paths.
  • Build validation runs PR builds; can be required or optional.
  • Comment resolution can require all comments addressed before merge.
  • GitHub uses branch protection rules with similar capabilities.

questions.title: Mono-repo vs Multi-repo
questions.scenario: A platform team manages 15 microservices. Teams want independent release cycles but need to share common libraries. CI builds are becoming slow due to repository size.
questions.questionText: What repository structure should you recommend?

choices.text: Multi-repo with shared packages published to artifact feed
Single mono-repo for all services and libraries
Separate repos with copy-paste of shared code
One repo per developer

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can teams release independently while still sharing common libraries in a controlled way?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use separate repositories per microservice for independent versioning and faster CI. Publish shared libraries as packages to Azure Artifacts or npm/NuGet feeds. Services depend on specific package versions, enabling controlled updates without repo coupling.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Mono-repo: single repo, atomic changes, but complex CI and scaling issues.
  • Multi-repo: independent repos, versioned dependencies, clearer ownership.
  • Semantic versioning for shared packages communicates breaking changes.
  • Consider mono-repo tooling (Nx, Bazel) if atomic cross-service changes are frequent.

questions.title: CI Pipeline Design
questions.scenario: A .NET application needs automated builds on every commit. Requirements: compile code, run unit tests, perform static code analysis, and publish artifacts for deployment.
questions.questionText: What is the correct order of CI pipeline stages?

choices.text: Publish artifacts, Build, Test
Test, Build, Analyze
Build only, defer other steps to CD
Restore dependencies, Build, Test, Analyze, Publish artifacts

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which steps depend on prior ones and what order fails fastest on errors.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: A proper CI pipeline: (1) Restore NuGet packages, (2) Build/compile code, (3) Run unit tests to catch bugs early, (4) Static code analysis for quality, (5) Publish build artifacts for CD pipelines. Fail fast: tests run before expensive analysis.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Fail fast: order steps by speed and likelihood of failure.
  • Parallelize independent tasks (unit tests, analysis) when possible.
  • Cache dependencies between builds to speed up restore.
  • Publish test results and code coverage for visibility.

questions.title: Build Agent Selection
questions.scenario: Your organization has strict security requirements: builds must run in your network, access internal package feeds, and have consistent pre-installed tools.
questions.questionText: Which build agent configuration should you use?

choices.text: Developer workstations as build agents
No agents; run builds manually
Self-hosted agents in your network with custom images
Microsoft-hosted agents only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which agent type lets you control the network environment, pre-installed tooling, and security posture?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Self-hosted agents run in your infrastructure with access to internal resources. You control the agent image, pre-installed tools, and security configuration. Microsoft-hosted agents are internet-facing and reset after each job, limiting internal access.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Self-hosted: persistent, customizable, network access; you manage updates.
  • Microsoft-hosted: clean image each job, no maintenance, limited customization.
  • Scale set agents auto-scale self-hosted agents based on queue.
  • Container-based agents provide consistent, reproducible environments.

questions.title: Pipeline as Code
questions.scenario: Your team wants pipeline definitions version-controlled alongside application code, with reusable templates across multiple projects.
questions.questionText: How should you implement pipeline as code?

choices.text: YAML pipelines with templates in a shared repository
Manual build steps documented in wiki
PowerShell scripts without pipeline definitions
Classic UI-based pipelines only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider which pipeline format lives alongside your code in source control and supports shared definitions.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: YAML pipelines store pipeline definitions as code in the repository, enabling version control, code review, and history. Templates in a shared repository provide reusable components (stages, jobs, steps) that multiple projects can reference, ensuring consistency.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Template types: step, job, stage, and variable templates.
  • Extends templates enforce organizational standards on all pipelines.
  • Template parameters enable customization while maintaining structure.
  • Store templates in a dedicated repo with versioned releases.

questions.title: Code Quality Gates
questions.scenario: You need to fail builds when code coverage drops below 80% or when new code quality issues are introduced.
questions.questionText: What tool integration should you implement?

choices.text: SonarQube with quality gates integrated into the pipeline
Compiler warnings treated as errors
Post-deployment quality checks
Manual code review only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What kind of tool can enforce coverage thresholds and quality standards as an automated pipeline gate?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: SonarQube (or SonarCloud) performs static code analysis, tracks code coverage, and enforces quality gates. Configure gates to fail when coverage drops below threshold or new issues exceed limits. Integrate as a pipeline task that blocks completion on gate failure.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Quality gates check: coverage, duplications, bugs, vulnerabilities, code smells.
  • "Leak period" focuses on new code quality, not legacy debt.
  • SonarCloud is SaaS; SonarQube is self-hosted.
  • Azure DevOps has built-in code coverage publishing; SonarQube adds deeper analysis.

questions.title: Release Pipeline Strategy
questions.scenario: Your application deploys to Dev, Test, and Production environments. Production deployments require manual approval and should only proceed after successful Test validation.
questions.questionText: How should you structure the release pipeline?

choices.text: Manual deployments to Production
Single stage deploying to all environments simultaneously
Separate pipelines per environment with no dependencies
Multi-stage pipeline with approval gates between Test and Production

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you enforce sequential environment progression with human sign-off before production?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Create stages for Dev, Test, and Production with sequential dependencies. Add approval checks before Production to require human sign-off. Conditions ensure Production only runs after Test succeeds. This provides traceability and control over production deployments.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Environments in Azure DevOps track deployment history and approvals.
  • Approval gates: manual approval, business hours, Azure Monitor alerts, REST API.
  • Use deployment jobs for environment-aware deployments.
  • YAML environments support checks, approvals, and locks.

questions.title: Blue-Green Deployment
questions.scenario: A customer-facing web application requires zero-downtime deployments with the ability to instantly rollback if issues are detected post-deployment.
questions.questionText: Which deployment strategy should you implement?

choices.text: Rolling deployment across all instances
Manual server-by-server updates
Blue-green deployment with traffic switching
In-place deployment with maintenance window

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which strategy uses a standby environment so you can switch traffic instantly and roll back just as fast?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Blue-green deployment runs two identical production environments. Deploy to inactive environment (green), validate, then switch traffic from active (blue). Rollback is instant: switch traffic back to blue. Azure App Service deployment slots provide built-in blue-green capability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• App Service slots: staging slot for green, production for blue; swap instantly.
  • Warm up the green slot before swap to avoid cold start issues.
  • Database migrations require backward compatibility for both versions.
  • Traffic Manager or Front Door can implement blue-green for VMs/AKS.

questions.title: Canary Deployment
questions.scenario: You want to reduce risk by deploying to a small percentage of users first, monitoring for errors, then gradually increasing traffic to the new version.
questions.questionText: Which deployment strategy provides gradual rollout with traffic control?

choices.text: Feature flags without infrastructure changes
Blue-green with full traffic switch
Rolling deployment to all instances
Canary deployment with traffic splitting

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about a strategy that lets you test with a small slice of real users before committing fully.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Canary deployment gradually shifts traffic to the new version (e.g., 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%). Monitor error rates and performance at each stage. If issues arise, traffic reverts to the stable version. App Service staging slots support traffic percentage routing.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• App Service slot traffic routing: configure percentage to staging slot.
  • AKS with service mesh (Istio) provides fine-grained traffic control.
  • Azure Front Door supports weighted routing for canary patterns.
  • Automate rollback based on Application Insights metrics thresholds.

questions.title: Feature Flags
questions.scenario: Product managers want to release features to specific users or regions without code deployments. Developers need to decouple deployment from feature release.
questions.questionText: What solution enables feature release independent of deployment?

choices.text: Azure App Configuration with feature flags
Environment variables per deployment
Compile-time feature toggles
Separate code branches per feature

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What service lets you toggle features at runtime for specific users without redeploying code?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure App Configuration feature management enables toggling features without redeployment. Define flags with targeting filters (users, groups, percentages). Code checks flag state at runtime. This decouples deployment (code in production) from release (feature enabled).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Targeting filters: percentage rollout, user/group targeting, time windows.
  • Feature flags should be short-lived; remove after full rollout.
  • LaunchDarkly is a popular third-party alternative with advanced targeting.
  • Technical debt: unused flags accumulate; track and clean up regularly.

questions.title: Database DevOps
questions.scenario: Your application uses Azure SQL Database. You need to automate schema changes, ensure backward compatibility during deployments, and enable rollback of database changes.
questions.questionText: How should you implement database DevOps?

choices.text: Manual SQL scripts run by DBAs
Direct production database modifications
State-based approach with SSDT and incremental deployments
Full database replacement with each deployment

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider a state-based approach where you define the desired schema and let tooling generate the diff scripts.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: SQL Server Data Tools (SSDT) uses a state-based approach: define desired schema state, generate incremental migration scripts. Include database project in CI/CD pipeline. Use pre/post deployment scripts for data migrations. Design changes for backward compatibility (expand-contract pattern).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• State-based (SSDT): define target state, auto-generate diff scripts.
  • Migration-based (EF Migrations, Flyway): explicit up/down migration scripts.
  • Expand-contract: add new column, migrate data, remove old column in separate releases.
  • Always test migrations against production-like data volumes.

questions.title: Secure Pipeline Secrets
questions.scenario: Your pipelines need access to connection strings, API keys, and certificates. Secrets must not be visible in logs, should be rotated regularly, and access must be audited.
questions.questionText: How should you manage pipeline secrets?

choices.text: Shared passwords in team documentation
Pipeline variables marked as secret
Azure Key Vault with variable group linking and managed identity access
Secrets in source code configuration files

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Where should secrets live so they can be rotated, audited, and fetched at runtime without appearing in pipeline definitions?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Store secrets in Azure Key Vault for centralized management, rotation, and auditing. Link Key Vault to Azure DevOps variable groups; secrets are fetched at runtime without exposure in pipeline definitions. Use managed identity for agent-to-Key Vault authentication.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Variable groups link to Key Vault; secrets sync automatically.
  • Secret variables are masked in logs (replaced with ***).
  • Service connections should use workload identity federation when possible.
  • Key Vault access policies or RBAC control who can read secrets.

questions.title: Dependency Scanning
questions.scenario: Your application uses open-source packages. You need to detect vulnerable dependencies in the build pipeline and block deployments when critical vulnerabilities are found.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: Manual review of package versions
Disable automatic package updates
Only use packages from trusted publishers
Software Composition Analysis (SCA) with Dependabot or WhiteSource

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What category of tooling automatically checks third-party packages against known vulnerability databases?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Software Composition Analysis tools (GitHub Dependabot, WhiteSource/Mend, Snyk) scan project dependencies against vulnerability databases. Integrate into CI pipeline to fail builds on critical CVEs. Dependabot can automatically create PRs to update vulnerable packages.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• OWASP Dependency-Check is an open-source alternative.
  • Configure severity thresholds: fail on critical/high, warn on medium.
  • Generate Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for compliance.
  • GitHub Advanced Security includes dependency scanning and secret scanning.

questions.title: Container Security
questions.scenario: Your team deploys containerized applications to AKS. You need to ensure base images are secure, scan for vulnerabilities, and prevent deployment of non-compliant images.
questions.questionText: What security measures should you implement?

choices.text: Public Docker Hub images without scanning
Azure Container Registry with Microsoft Defender, image scanning, and admission control
Build images locally without registry
Disable image pulls to prevent vulnerabilities

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about a private registry with scanning plus a cluster-side gate that blocks non-compliant images.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Container Registry stores images privately. Microsoft Defender for Containers scans images for vulnerabilities. Configure AKS admission control (Azure Policy/Gatekeeper) to block deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities or from untrusted registries.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use minimal base images (Alpine, distroless) to reduce attack surface.
  • ACR Tasks can rebuild images when base images are updated.
  • Image signing with Notation ensures image integrity and provenance.
  • Quarantine pattern: images go to quarantine registry until scanned clean.

questions.title: Service Connection Security
questions.scenario: Pipelines need to deploy to Azure subscriptions. You want to limit which pipelines can access production, use minimal permissions, and avoid long-lived credentials.
questions.questionText: How should you configure service connections?

choices.text: Personal Azure credentials in pipelines
Workload identity federation with scoped RBAC and pipeline restrictions
Shared service principal password in variable group
Single service principal with Owner access for all pipelines

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can you authenticate pipelines to Azure without storing any long-lived credentials?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Use workload identity federation for service connections (no stored secrets). Grant minimal RBAC permissions (Contributor on specific resource groups, not subscription Owner). Restrict service connection usage to specific pipelines/environments to prevent unauthorized access to production.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Workload identity: Azure DevOps/GitHub tokens exchanged for Azure AD tokens.
  • Service connection approvals and checks add governance controls.
  • Separate service connections for production vs. non-production.
  • Service principal certificates are more secure than secrets if WIF unavailable.

questions.title: Secure Development Lifecycle
questions.scenario: Your organization needs to integrate security throughout the development lifecycle: threat modeling during design, security testing during development, and compliance verification before release.
questions.questionText: What practice encompasses this security-first approach?

choices.text: Security review only before production
Separate security team post-deployment
DevSecOps with shift-left security practices
Penetration testing annually

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which philosophy weaves security into every stage of delivery rather than treating it as a final gate?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: DevSecOps integrates security practices into DevOps workflows. Shift-left security moves testing earlier: threat modeling in design, SAST in development, SCA for dependencies, DAST in test environments. Security becomes everyone's responsibility, not a final gate.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SAST (Static Application Security Testing): analyze source code.
  • DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): test running applications.
  • IAST (Interactive): combines SAST and DAST during testing.
  • Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle (SDL) provides a framework.

questions.title: Infrastructure as Code Tools
questions.scenario: Your team needs to provision Azure infrastructure reproducibly. They want declarative syntax, state management, and integration with Azure DevOps pipelines.
questions.questionText: Which IaC approach should you recommend for Azure?

choices.text: Bicep with Azure DevOps pipeline tasks
Manual Azure Portal configuration
Imperative PowerShell scripts
Azure CLI commands in documentation

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about a declarative approach purpose-built for Azure that can plug directly into your CI/CD pipeline.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Bicep is Azure's domain-specific language for infrastructure, compiling to ARM templates. It offers cleaner syntax, modules, and excellent tooling. Azure DevOps has native Bicep tasks for deployment. Terraform is a multi-cloud alternative with its own state management.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Bicep: Azure-native, no state file, idempotent, what-if previews.
  • Terraform: multi-cloud, state file required, larger ecosystem.
  • Bicep modules enable reusable, parameterized infrastructure components.
  • Deployment stacks provide lifecycle management for Bicep deployments.

questions.title: Terraform State Management
questions.scenario: Your team uses Terraform for multi-cloud infrastructure. Multiple team members need to collaborate, and state must be protected from corruption and unauthorized access.
questions.questionText: How should you manage Terraform state?

choices.text: No state management; recreate infrastructure each time
Shared network drive for state files
Azure Storage backend with state locking and access controls
Local state files committed to Git

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When multiple people run infrastructure changes, what prevents them from corrupting shared state?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Store Terraform state in Azure Storage account with blob lease locking to prevent concurrent modifications. Enable versioning for state history. Use RBAC and network restrictions to control access. State contains sensitive data; treat it as a protected resource.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• State locking prevents "terraform apply" race conditions.
  • Enable storage account versioning for state recovery.
  • State may contain secrets; encrypt and restrict access.
  • Terraform Cloud/Enterprise provides managed state with additional features.

questions.title: Configuration Management
questions.scenario: VMs provisioned by IaC need consistent software installation, configuration files, and ongoing drift detection to maintain compliance.
questions.questionText: What tool provides desired state configuration for VMs?

choices.text: Manual RDP sessions for each VM
Custom startup scripts only
Azure Automanage with machine configuration (formerly Guest Configuration)
Golden images with no post-deployment configuration

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What Azure-native capability can continuously audit VM configuration and remediate drift over time?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Automanage machine configuration (formerly Azure Policy Guest Configuration) uses PowerShell DSC to define desired state. It audits VMs for compliance and can remediate drift. Integrate with Azure Policy for governance at scale across all VMs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Machine configuration packages contain DSC resources and assignments.
  • Audit mode reports compliance; enforce mode remediates drift.
  • Ansible, Chef, Puppet are cross-platform alternatives.
  • Combine with VM extensions for initial configuration during provisioning.

questions.title: GitOps for Kubernetes
questions.scenario: Your AKS cluster configurations should be version-controlled, with automatic synchronization from Git to the cluster. Changes should be auditable and reversible.
questions.questionText: What approach should you implement?

choices.text: Manual kubectl apply from developer machines
GitOps with Flux or Argo CD
Azure DevOps pipelines with kubectl in every deployment
Azure Portal configuration only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What if a cluster-side operator continuously reconciled its state with whatever is committed in a Git repo?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GitOps treats Git as the single source of truth for cluster configuration. Operators like Flux (built into AKS as an extension) continuously reconcile cluster state with Git repository. Changes are made via Git commits, providing audit trail and easy rollback via git revert.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Flux v2 is the CNCF GitOps toolkit; native AKS extension available.
  • Argo CD provides UI and advanced deployment strategies.
  • GitOps: pull-based (operator pulls from Git); traditional CI/CD: push-based.
  • Separate repos for app code and cluster config (config repo pattern).

questions.title: Application Performance Monitoring
questions.scenario: Your web application needs end-to-end monitoring: request tracing, dependency tracking, exception logging, and performance metrics with alerting.
questions.questionText: Which Azure service provides comprehensive APM capabilities?

choices.text: Windows Event Logs
Azure Monitor metrics only
Custom logging to blob storage
Application Insights with distributed tracing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which Azure service offers end-to-end request tracing, dependency mapping, and anomaly detection out of the box?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Application Insights is Azure's APM solution. It automatically tracks requests, dependencies (SQL, HTTP calls), exceptions, and custom metrics. Distributed tracing follows requests across services. Smart detection alerts on anomalies. Live metrics show real-time performance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Auto-instrumentation available for .NET, Java, Node.js, Python.
  • OpenTelemetry is becoming the standard; App Insights supports OTLP.
  • Application Map visualizes service dependencies and health.
  • Workspace-based App Insights uses Log Analytics for unified querying.

questions.title: Deployment Monitoring
questions.scenario: After each deployment, you need to automatically verify the application is healthy. If errors exceed thresholds, the deployment should automatically roll back.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: No post-deployment validation
User-reported issues for rollback decisions
Deployment gates with Azure Monitor alerts and automatic rollback
Manual verification after each deployment

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can a pipeline automatically verify post-deployment health and revert if metrics go red?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Configure post-deployment gates that query Azure Monitor alerts or Application Insights metrics. If error rates or latency exceed thresholds, gates fail. Combine with Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions deployment protection rules to automatically trigger rollback to the previous version.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure Monitor alerts can be gate conditions in release pipelines.
  • REST API gates can query custom health endpoints.
  • App Service auto-heal can rollback individual instances based on request failures.
  • Implement health check endpoints following Azure Load Balancer patterns.

questions.title: Feedback Loops
questions.scenario: You want to close the DevOps loop by automatically creating work items from production issues and feeding user feedback into the development process.
questions.questionText: What integration should you implement?

choices.text: Application Insights work item integration and user feedback widgets
Manual bug triage from email reports
No connection between operations and development
Separate systems for dev and ops

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can production telemetry automatically feed issues back into the development backlog?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Application Insights integrates with Azure DevOps to create work items from detected issues, including exception details and diagnostic context. Feedback widgets in applications capture user-reported issues. This closes the feedback loop between production and development.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Smart detection automatically identifies anomalies and can create alerts.
  • Work item templates include App Insights data for context.
  • Release annotations mark deployments in App Insights for correlation.
  • Implement feature flags to quickly disable problematic features.

questions.title: Log Aggregation
questions.scenario: Your microservices application needs centralized logging across all services. Developers need to search and correlate logs from multiple services to troubleshoot issues.
questions.questionText: What logging architecture should you implement?

choices.text: Separate logging systems per service
Console output without persistence
Structured logging to Log Analytics workspace with correlation IDs
Local log files on each container

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What makes it possible to trace a single request across many services in a centralized log store?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Send structured logs (JSON format) from all services to a centralized Log Analytics workspace. Include correlation IDs (trace ID, span ID) in every log entry to trace requests across services. Use Kusto Query Language (KQL) to search, filter, and correlate logs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• OpenTelemetry provides standard correlation headers (W3C Trace Context).
  • Structured logging enables field-based queries vs. text parsing.
  • Container Insights collects stdout/stderr from AKS containers.
  • Log retention policies balance cost and compliance requirements.

questions.title: Test Automation Strategy
questions.scenario: Your pipeline needs multiple test types: unit tests for fast feedback, integration tests for component interaction, and UI tests for end-to-end validation.
questions.questionText: How should you organize tests in the pipeline?

choices.text: Manual testing only
Only UI tests for complete coverage
Skip tests to speed up deployment
Test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, minimal UI tests

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The test pyramid optimizes for fast feedback with unit tests and reduces slow, brittle UI tests.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The test pyramid recommends: many fast unit tests (base), moderate integration tests (middle), few slow UI/E2E tests (top). Unit tests run in CI for fast feedback. Integration tests validate component interactions. UI tests verify critical user journeys. This balances coverage with speed.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Unit tests: isolated, fast, run on every commit.
  • Integration tests: test contracts between services, can use test containers.
  • E2E tests: slow, brittle; reserve for critical paths.
  • Parallelize test execution to reduce pipeline duration.

questions.title: Kubernetes Deployment Strategy
questions.scenario: Your AKS application needs zero-downtime deployments with the ability to quickly rollback. Pods should be updated gradually with health checks.
questions.questionText: Which Kubernetes deployment strategy should you configure?

choices.text: Recreate strategy (stop all, then start new)
Rolling update with readiness probes and rollback capability
Manual pod deletion and recreation
Single replica with downtime during updates

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which Kubernetes strategy replaces pods incrementally while verifying each new pod is ready for traffic?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Kubernetes rolling update strategy updates pods incrementally. Configure maxSurge (extra pods during update) and maxUnavailable (pods that can be down). Readiness probes determine when new pods are ready for traffic. kubectl rollout undo enables quick rollback to previous revision.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Readiness probes: determine if pod should receive traffic.
  • Liveness probes: determine if pod should be restarted.
  • Startup probes: for slow-starting containers.
  • Blue-green and canary require service mesh or ingress controller support.

questions.title: Git Hooks
questions.scenario: You want to enforce code formatting and run linting before commits are created, preventing poorly formatted code from entering the repository.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: Pre-commit hooks with formatters and linters (using Husky or similar)
Manual code review for formatting only
Post-merge formatting by CI
No formatting enforcement

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What is the earliest point in the developer workflow where you can catch formatting violations automatically?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Git pre-commit hooks run scripts before commit creation. Tools like Husky (Node.js) or pre-commit (Python) manage hooks. Configure to run formatters (Prettier, Black) and linters (ESLint, Pylint). Issues are caught locally, reducing CI failures and code review friction.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• lint-staged runs linters only on staged files for speed.
  • Pre-commit hooks can be bypassed with --no-verify; CI provides backup.
  • Commit message hooks can enforce conventional commits format.
  • EditorConfig ensures consistent settings across IDEs.

questions.title: Build Caching
questions.scenario: Your CI builds take 15 minutes due to dependency downloads and compilation. You need to reduce build times while maintaining build correctness.
questions.questionText: What optimization should you implement?

choices.text: Longer build timeouts without optimization
Skip dependency restoration on each build
Reduce test coverage to speed up builds
Pipeline caching for dependencies and build outputs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What technique avoids re-downloading the same packages on every build by reusing prior results?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions support pipeline caching. Cache package manager directories (node_modules, .nuget, .gradle) keyed by lock file hash. Cache build outputs for incremental compilation. This dramatically reduces build time while ensuring correctness through cache key invalidation.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cache key: hash of lock file ensures cache invalidates on dependency changes.
  • Docker layer caching speeds up container builds.
  • GitHub Actions: actions/cache; Azure DevOps: Cache task.
  • Self-hosted agents can use persistent caches for even faster builds.

questions.title: Artifact Management
questions.scenario: Your organization produces npm packages, NuGet libraries, and container images. Teams need to share packages internally and control which external packages are allowed.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: Azure Artifacts with upstream sources and package policies
Email package files between teams
File shares for package distribution
Direct downloads from public registries only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Where can teams publish internal packages and control which external packages are consumed?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Artifacts hosts npm, NuGet, Maven, Python, and universal packages. Upstream sources cache packages from public registries, providing availability and security scanning. Feed permissions control who can publish and consume. Views (like @release) control package promotion.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Upstream sources: cache external packages; block if removed from public.
  • Views: promote packages through quality stages (@prerelease, @release).
  • ACR (Azure Container Registry) for container images; separate from Artifacts.
  • Retention policies manage storage costs for old package versions.

questions.title: SAST Integration
questions.scenario: Your security team requires static code analysis to detect security vulnerabilities like SQL injection and XSS before code reaches production.
questions.questionText: What should you integrate into your pipeline?

choices.text: Manual security code review only
SAST tools (GitHub Advanced Security, SonarQube, or Checkmarx) in CI
Security testing in production
Penetration testing replacing code analysis

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What type of analysis examines source code for security flaws without executing the application?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools analyze source code without execution. They detect patterns like SQL injection, XSS, and insecure deserialization. Integrate into CI pipeline to fail builds on critical findings. GitHub Advanced Security CodeQL, SonarQube, and Checkmarx are common options.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SAST complements SCA (dependencies) and DAST (runtime).
  • False positives require tuning; focus on high-confidence findings.
  • GitHub CodeQL supports custom queries for organization-specific rules.
  • Incremental analysis scans only changed code for faster feedback.

questions.title: Environment Consistency
questions.scenario: Developers complain that code works locally but fails in test environments. You need to ensure consistency between development, test, and production environments.
questions.questionText: What approach ensures environment consistency?

choices.text: Containerization with identical images across all environments
Manual environment configuration documentation
Different configurations per environment without tracking
Virtual machines with ad-hoc installations

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What packaging approach guarantees the same runtime, libraries, and code travel together across every environment?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Containerization (Docker) packages application code, runtime, and dependencies into an immutable image. The same image runs in development (Docker Desktop), test (AKS/ACI), and production (AKS). Environment differences are limited to configuration (environment variables, secrets), not the application itself.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Docker Compose enables local development with multi-container setups.
  • Dev Containers (VS Code) provide consistent developer environments.
  • External configuration (environment variables, mounted configs) varies by environment.
  • Image promotion: same image through dev -> test -> prod; never rebuild.

questions.title: Deployment Rings
questions.scenario: Your application serves millions of users globally. You want to minimize blast radius by deploying to progressively larger user groups, validating health at each stage.
questions.questionText: What deployment pattern should you implement?

choices.text: Simultaneous deployment to all users
Ring-based deployment with progressive exposure
Geographic deployment without validation
A/B testing without deployment stages

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about concentric circles of exposure, starting with the smallest audience and expanding outward.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Ring-based deployment defines concentric deployment stages: Ring 0 (internal/dogfood), Ring 1 (canary users), Ring 2 (early adopters), Ring 3 (all users). Each ring validates stability before expanding. This limits blast radius and enables early detection of issues before they affect all users.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Microsoft uses rings internally for Windows and Azure deployments.
  • Ring criteria: internal employees, beta users, percentage rollout.
  • Bake time: wait period at each ring to observe metrics.
  • Feature flags can implement logical rings without infrastructure changes.

questions.title: Inner Source
questions.scenario: Your organization has multiple teams that could benefit from sharing and contributing to internal projects. You want to enable cross-team collaboration while maintaining code ownership.
questions.questionText: What practice should you adopt?

choices.text: Copy code between repositories
All code in a single team's ownership
Inner source with discoverable repositories and contribution guidelines
Strict team silos with no code sharing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What if you applied open-source collaboration norms — discoverability, contribution guidelines, PRs — inside the company?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Inner source adopts open-source collaboration practices internally. Make repositories discoverable, document contribution guidelines (CONTRIBUTING.md), accept pull requests from other teams, and maintain clear ownership (CODEOWNERS). This enables reuse and collective improvement while preserving accountability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CODEOWNERS file defines required reviewers for specific paths.
  • README, CONTRIBUTING, and LICENSE files set expectations.
  • Trusted committers are non-owners with merge permissions.
  • GitHub/GitLab enterprise features support inner source patterns.

questions.title: SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs
questions.scenario: Your team needs to define measurable service reliability targets, track them, and alert when the service degrades below acceptable thresholds.
questions.questionText: What framework should you implement?

choices.text: Define SLIs (metrics), set SLOs (targets), track error budgets
Arbitrary uptime targets without measurement
React to outages without proactive monitoring
100% availability target for all services

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you quantify reliability, set acceptable thresholds, and know when to slow down releases?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Service Level Indicators (SLIs) are specific metrics (latency, error rate, availability). Service Level Objectives (SLOs) are target values for SLIs (99.9% availability). Error budget is the allowed unreliability (0.1%). When error budget depletes, slow down releases to focus on reliability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SLI examples: request latency p99, error rate, throughput.
  • SLO: internal target; SLA: contractual commitment with consequences.
  • Error budget policy defines actions when budget is consumed.
  • Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) principles guide this framework.

questions.title: Multi-Stage Docker Builds
questions.scenario: Your Docker images are large because they include build tools and source code. You need smaller production images with only runtime dependencies.
questions.questionText: What technique should you use?

choices.text: Single Dockerfile with all dependencies
Manual cleanup of build artifacts
Multi-stage Docker builds with separate build and runtime stages
Larger base images with everything pre-installed

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can you separate the build toolchain from the final image so production carries only what it needs to run?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Multi-stage Dockerfile has separate stages: build stage with SDK/compilers produces artifacts, then a runtime stage with minimal base image copies only the compiled output. Final image contains only runtime dependencies, reducing size, attack surface, and pull time.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Example: build with mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk, runtime with dotnet/aspnet.
  • Distroless images contain only the application; no shell or package manager.
  • Layer ordering matters: put infrequently changing layers first for caching.
  • BuildKit enables parallel stage building and better caching.

questions.title: Secret Scanning
questions.scenario: Developers occasionally commit secrets like API keys or passwords to Git. You need to detect and alert on secrets in code before they're exposed.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: Secret scanning in CI and pre-commit hooks (GitHub Secret Scanning, gitleaks)
Rotate all credentials after each release
Trust developers to never commit secrets
Review all commits manually for secrets

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What automated approach catches credentials that slip into commits before they reach the remote repository?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Secret scanning tools (GitHub Secret Scanning, GitLeaks, TruffleHog) detect patterns matching API keys, tokens, and passwords. Run in pre-commit hooks for immediate feedback and in CI as a safety net. GitHub Advanced Security provides push protection to block secrets before they're pushed.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GitHub Secret Scanning: native integration, partner alerts notify providers.
  • Push protection blocks the push if secrets are detected.
  • Git history contains deleted secrets; use BFG or git-filter-repo to purge.
  • Rotate any credential that was ever committed, even if removed.

questions.title: Immutable Infrastructure
questions.scenario: Your team frequently patches production servers, leading to configuration drift and "works on my machine" issues. You want consistent, reproducible infrastructure.
questions.questionText: What approach should you adopt?

choices.text: Manual server configuration from documentation
Immutable infrastructure with image-based deployments
Long-running servers with cumulative patches
Ignore drift and fix in next major release

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What paradigm treats servers as disposable — never patched in place, always replaced with a fresh image?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Immutable infrastructure treats servers as disposable. Instead of patching running servers, build new images (VM images, containers) with updates and replace the old infrastructure. This eliminates configuration drift, ensures reproducibility, and simplifies rollback (deploy previous image).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Containers are inherently immutable; new version = new container.
  • VM images: use Packer to build golden images from code.
  • Blue-green deployment complements immutable infrastructure.
  • State (databases, storage) must be external to immutable compute.

questions.title: Dashboards and Visualization
questions.scenario: Stakeholders need visibility into deployment frequency, lead time, failure rate, and mean time to recovery. Development teams need operational dashboards.
questions.questionText: What metrics and visualizations should you provide?

choices.text: No metrics tracking
Only production incident counts
Manual spreadsheet reporting
DORA metrics dashboards with Azure DevOps analytics and Grafana

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Which well-known framework defines the four key metrics that predict software delivery performance?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) metrics: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, Mean Time to Recovery. Azure DevOps Analytics and Power BI can visualize pipeline metrics. Grafana dashboards combine infrastructure and application metrics for operational visibility.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• DORA research identifies these four metrics as predictors of software delivery performance.
  • Elite performers: multiple deploys/day, <1 hour lead time, <15% failure rate, <1 hour MTTR.
  • Azure DevOps has built-in Analytics with OData queries.
  • GitHub Insights provides similar repository and workflow metrics.

questions.title: Matrix Builds
questions.scenario: Your library needs to be tested against multiple versions of Node.js (16, 18, 20) and multiple operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS).
questions.questionText: How should you configure the CI pipeline?

choices.text: Test only on one configuration
Manual testing on each environment
Separate pipelines for each combination
Matrix strategy with version and OS combinations

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How can a single pipeline definition automatically fan out across every version-and-OS combination?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Matrix strategy defines variables (node: [16, 18, 20], os: [ubuntu, windows, macos]) and runs jobs for each combination. This provides comprehensive coverage without duplicating pipeline code. Jobs run in parallel for fast feedback. Exclude specific combinations if needed.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GitHub Actions: strategy.matrix; Azure DevOps: matrix in job strategy.
  • Use fail-fast: false to continue other matrix jobs if one fails.
  • Exclude specific combinations that aren't needed.
  • Include additional variables for specific matrix entries.

questions.title: Release Notes Automation
questions.scenario: Product management wants automated release notes generated from commits and work items for each release.
questions.questionText: How should you automate release notes?

choices.text: Copy commit messages verbatim
Manual release notes written before each release
No release notes
Conventional commits with automated changelog generation

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What commit message convention makes it possible for tools to auto-generate changelogs and bump versions?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Conventional Commits format (feat:, fix:, docs:) enables tools to parse commit messages and generate changelogs. Tools like semantic-release, standard-version, or release-drafter automate version bumping and release notes. Link commits to work items for traceability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Format: type(scope): description. Types: feat, fix, docs, chore, etc.
  • Breaking changes: BREAKING CHANGE: footer or ! after type.
  • Semantic versioning: feat = minor, fix = patch, BREAKING = major.
  • GitHub releases and Azure DevOps release notes can be auto-generated.

questions.title: Policy as Code
questions.scenario: Your organization needs to enforce infrastructure compliance: all storage accounts must have encryption, all VMs must be in specific regions, and all resources must have required tags.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: Post-deployment compliance scripts
Manual review of all deployments
Azure Policy with deny effects and compliance reporting
Documentation of requirements only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What Azure-native mechanism can block resource creation that violates organizational compliance rules?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Policy defines compliance rules as code. Policies with deny effect block non-compliant resources at deployment time. Audit effect reports non-compliance without blocking. Assign policies at management group level for organization-wide enforcement. Compliance dashboard shows status across subscriptions.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Built-in policies cover common scenarios; custom policies use JSON definitions.
  • Policy initiatives bundle related policies for assignment.
  • DeployIfNotExists can auto-remediate (e.g., enable diagnostics).
  • Version-control policy definitions alongside infrastructure code.

questions.title: Pipeline Permissions
questions.scenario: You need to control which pipelines can access sensitive service connections, environments, and variable groups.
questions.questionText: How should you configure pipeline security?

choices.text: All pipelines access all resources
Single shared service account for all pipelines
Security through obscurity
Resource restrictions and approval checks on protected resources

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you ensure only authorized pipelines can touch production service connections and environments?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure DevOps allows restricting service connections, variable groups, and environments to specific pipelines. Add approval checks on environments requiring sign-off before deployment. This prevents unauthorized pipelines from accessing production resources or secrets.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Pipeline permissions: Open (any pipeline) or Restricted (specific pipelines).
  • Environment checks: approvals, business hours, branch control.
  • Variable groups can require approval before use.
  • Secure files require explicit pipeline authorization.

questions.title: Chaos Engineering
questions.scenario: You want to proactively test your system's resilience by introducing controlled failures in production to discover weaknesses before they cause outages.
questions.questionText: What practice should you implement?

choices.text: Chaos engineering with Azure Chaos Studio experiments
Never test in production
Wait for production failures to test resilience
Disable redundancy to test recovery

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What practice proactively injects controlled faults to discover weaknesses before real outages do?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Chaos engineering intentionally injects failures (pod kills, network latency, VM shutdown) to test resilience. Azure Chaos Studio provides managed chaos experiments with safety controls. Start with non-production, then carefully extend to production with blast radius limits. Validates that failover, retry logic, and alerts work correctly.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Chaos Studio experiments: define faults, targets, duration, and safety stops.
  • Common faults: CPU pressure, network disconnect, service kill, DNS failure.
  • GameDay: scheduled chaos exercises with team observation.
  • Principles: start small, minimize blast radius, have a hypothesis.

questions.title: Infrastructure Deployment Pipeline
questions.scenario: Your IaC code needs the same rigor as application code: validation, testing, approval for production, and change tracking.
questions.questionText: How should you deploy infrastructure changes?

choices.text: PR-based workflow with validation, what-if preview, and staged deployment
Direct deployment from developer machines
Azure Portal changes with manual documentation
Single branch with immediate production deployment

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about applying the same rigor to infrastructure changes as to application code: review, preview, then deploy.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Treat infrastructure code like application code. PRs trigger validation (syntax, linting). What-if/plan shows proposed changes without applying. Deploy to lower environments first, then production with approval. This provides change review, safe deployment, and audit trail.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Bicep/ARM what-if: preview changes without deployment.
  • Terraform plan: show proposed changes; apply requires approval.
  • Policy compliance check as pipeline gate before deployment.
  • Drift detection: compare deployed state to code regularly.

questions.title: Code Review Best Practices
questions.scenario: Code reviews are becoming bottlenecks with long review times and inconsistent feedback. You need to improve review efficiency and quality.
questions.questionText: What practices should you implement?

choices.text: Skip reviews for urgent changes
Large PRs reviewed by many people
Small PRs, automated checks, review guidelines, and CODEOWNERS
Only senior developers review code

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Small PRs are faster to review; automation catches style issues; guidelines ensure consistency.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Keep PRs small and focused (< 400 lines). Automate style/lint checks so reviewers focus on logic. Document review guidelines (what to look for, response time expectations). CODEOWNERS automatically assigns appropriate reviewers. Use PR templates to ensure context is provided.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Research shows review quality drops significantly after 400 lines.
  • Stacked PRs: chain of dependent PRs for large changes.
  • Review time SLO: set expectations (e.g., first response within 24 hours).
  • Use suggestion feature for minor changes instead of comments.

questions.title: Monorepo CI Optimization
questions.scenario: Your monorepo contains 20 services. Currently, all services build on every commit, causing long CI times. You want to build only affected services.
questions.questionText: What optimization should you implement?

choices.text: Path-based triggers and affected project detection
Random selection of services to build
Build all services regardless of changes
Disable CI for faster development

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you avoid rebuilding all 20 services when only one service's files actually changed?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Configure path-based triggers so pipelines run only when their service's files change. Use monorepo tools (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel) to detect affected projects including dependencies. This dramatically reduces CI time by building only what changed and what depends on it.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure DevOps: trigger paths include/exclude patterns.
  • Nx/Turborepo: affected command detects changed projects and dependencies.
  • Distributed caching: share build outputs across CI runs and developers.
  • Task orchestration: parallel execution respecting dependency graph.

questions.title: Supply Chain Security
questions.scenario: You need to ensure the integrity of your software supply chain: verify that artifacts haven't been tampered with and that dependencies come from trusted sources.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: SBOM generation, artifact signing, and dependency verification
Trust all public packages
Manual artifact inspection
Disable dependency updates

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you prove what went into your artifact and that nobody tampered with it after the build?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Generate Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) listing all dependencies. Sign build artifacts (containers with Notation, binaries with code signing) to prove integrity and origin. Verify dependency signatures and checksums. Use private feeds with upstream caching to control package sources.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SBOM formats: SPDX, CycloneDX; required by some regulations.
  • SLSA framework defines supply chain security levels.
  • Sigstore provides keyless signing for open source.
  • Package lock files ensure reproducible builds with exact versions.

questions.title: Incident Management
questions.scenario: When production incidents occur, your team needs clear escalation paths, communication channels, and post-incident learning processes.
questions.questionText: What should you implement?

choices.text: Ignore incidents until customers complain
Management handles all incidents
On-call rotation, incident response runbooks, and blameless postmortems
Ad-hoc response by whoever is available

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Structured incident management includes defined roles, runbooks, and learning from incidents.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Establish on-call rotation with clear escalation paths. Create runbooks documenting common incident responses. During incidents, use defined roles (incident commander, communications). After resolution, conduct blameless postmortems focusing on systemic improvements, not individual blame.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• PagerDuty, OpsGenie integrate with Azure Monitor for alerting.
  • Incident severity levels define response urgency and communication.
  • Postmortem template: timeline, impact, root cause, action items.
  • Track action items to completion; incidents repeat without fixes.

questions.title: Multi-Cloud Deployment
questions.scenario: Your organization deploys applications to both Azure and AWS. You need consistent deployment practices and shared pipeline components across both clouds.
questions.questionText: How should you design the deployment architecture?

choices.text: Common pipeline templates with cloud-specific deployment stages
Completely separate teams and pipelines per cloud
Single cloud only, ignore multi-cloud requirement
Manual deployments to each cloud

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you keep build and test steps consistent while allowing the deploy step to differ per cloud provider?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Create reusable pipeline templates for common steps (build, test, scan). Cloud-specific deployment stages handle Azure vs AWS differences. Use Terraform for multi-cloud IaC with provider-specific modules. Store cloud credentials as separate service connections with appropriate access controls.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Terraform: single language, multiple providers for multi-cloud IaC.
  • Kubernetes (AKS, EKS): consistent workload deployment across clouds.
  • Abstract cloud-specific details behind common interfaces.
  • GitHub Actions/Azure DevOps work with both Azure and AWS.

gl-ci.name: Continuous Integration (CI)
gl-ci.definition: Practice of frequently merging code changes into a shared repository, with automated builds and tests validating each change.
gl-ci.examNote: CI catches integration issues early; key metrics include build frequency and failure rate.

gl-cd.name: Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD)
gl-cd.definition: Continuous Delivery ensures code is always deployable; Continuous Deployment automatically deploys every passing change to production.
gl-cd.examNote: Delivery requires manual approval for production; Deployment is fully automated.

gl-dora.name: DORA Metrics
gl-dora.definition: Four key metrics predicting software delivery performance: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time, Change Failure Rate, Mean Time to Recovery.
gl-dora.examNote: Elite performers deploy multiple times daily with less than 15% failure rate.

gl-gitops.name: GitOps
gl-gitops.definition: Operational model using Git as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications, with automated synchronization.
gl-gitops.examNote: Flux and Argo CD are common GitOps operators for Kubernetes.

gl-shift-left.name: Shift-Left Security
gl-shift-left.definition: Practice of moving security testing earlier in the development lifecycle, integrating into development and CI rather than waiting for pre-production.
gl-shift-left.examNote: SAST, SCA, and secret scanning are shift-left practices.

gl-blue-green.name: Blue-Green Deployment
gl-blue-green.definition: Deployment strategy maintaining two identical environments, switching traffic between them for zero-downtime deployments and instant rollback.
gl-blue-green.examNote: App Service deployment slots provide built-in blue-green capability.

gl-canary.name: Canary Deployment
gl-canary.definition: Deployment strategy gradually routing increasing percentages of traffic to a new version while monitoring for issues.
gl-canary.examNote: Reduces blast radius by exposing new versions to small user groups first.

gl-iac.name: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
gl-iac.definition: Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable definition files rather than manual configuration.
gl-iac.examNote: Bicep is Azure-native; Terraform is multi-cloud.
